sub.en: Some verbs describe a state, not an action. Which form does each sentence need?

items.q: I ___ this is a real bargain.
items.why: think = have an opinion. That is a state, so the simple form is used.

items.why: Here think = use your mind, which is an action, so the continuous is possible.

items.why: belong is a state verb and has no continuous form.

items.q: Sorry, I ___ you — have we met?

items.why: sell is an action verb, so the continuous works normally.

have = eat is an action, so the continuous is correct here.
see = understand is a state; see = meet is an action.

acts.title: Why we spend
text: Every November, in the run-up to the winter holidays, the shops fill with special offers. Items that were full price in October are suddenly half-price, and a queue forms outside the door before it opens. Most consumers believe that they are making a sensible purchase. They are not always right.

Psychologists who study spending say that a bargain does something strange to us. When we see a deal, we stop asking whether we want the item and start asking how much we are saving. We prefer the feeling of winning to the object itself. That is why so many people admit, a week later, that they do not really understand why they bought it.

There is also the question of what a low price hides. Cheap goods have to be transported a long way, which is harmful to the environment, and the workers who make them rarely have secure jobs. In some countries the sales themselves have become dangerous: shops have reported injuries in the crowd, and security staff now control the doors.

This is where Buy Nothing Day comes in. The idea belongs to a Canadian movement that began more than twenty years ago and now exists in over sixty countries. It asks one simple thing: for twenty-four hours, buy nothing at all. Supporters do not think that a single day changes the world. They mean something smaller and more useful — that most of us have never tried to go a whole day without spending, and that trying it teaches us something about ourselves.
Not everyone is convinced. Critics argue that guilt-free brands and money given to charity do more good than a day of doing nothing. But nobody who has actually tried it says that it proves nothing.

items.s: The text says shoppers are always right about what is worth buying.
According to the text, a bargain changes the question we ask ourselves.
The text says cheap goods usually travel a long way before they are sold.
Buy Nothing Day began in Canada.
Supporters of Buy Nothing Day claim that one day will change the world.
Everybody agrees that Buy Nothing Day is the best idea.

tts: Today is one of the busiest shopping days of the year, and this centre is full of people.
But something different is happening here. It is Buy Nothing Day, and Lewis is standing in the main entrance with a sign that says: Stop Shopping, Start Living.
The idea is simple. We are asking everybody to think about their spending habits and buy nothing at all for one day.
When you really think about it, the idea of buying things as a way of spending your leisure time is crazy. We believe shopping makes us happy, but it does not.
Only twenty per cent of the world’s population is consuming over eighty per cent of the Earth’s natural resources.
Something might seem a great bargain, but that can be because it was made where the workers are not paid enough. Transporting goods by air is also harmful.
Most people do not understand how difficult it is to last twenty-four hours without spending any money.
It started in Canada more than twenty years ago, and now there are Buy Nothing Day movements in over sixty-five countries.

write.q: Write about the last thing you bought that you did not really need. Use at least four state verbs (think, believe, prefer, realize, admit, mean, belong, own, understand) and one action use of a state verb (I am having…, I am thinking about…).
plan: why it looked like a bargain
write.model: I have to admit that I bought a second coat in the January sales. It was half-price, and I thought that made it a bargain. I already own two, so I did not need it. When I got home I realized I had bought the feeling of saving money, not the coat. I still prefer my old one. I am thinking about giving the new one to charity — I am convinced somebody else needs it more than I do.

speak.q: Talk for about a minute: do you agree that most people buy things they do not need? Use “It depends on…”, “I don’t think so” and “I’m convinced that…”.
speak.model: I think most people do buy things they don’t need, but it depends on the person. My mother owns almost nothing and gives what she can to charity. I’m the opposite — I have to admit I love a special offer. I’m convinced that the run-up to a big sale changes the way I think. I see a deal and I stop asking whether I want the item.
